findings.message: Alias generic bounds are ignored when building the public type surface. A `TypeAlias` whose generic bound exposes a prohibited role is therefore accepted by `CompositionRootPureDi`; include `generics` in the collected bound types.

Primitive linting scans only the alias target and skips `TypeAlias.generics`, so primitives nested in alias bounds are never reported at the `Bound` position. Collect the alias generic bounds alongside the target slot.

`generics` is an unconstrained `Vec`, and the linter changes only scan its bounds; nothing rejects duplicate parameter names. Consequently, `TypeAlias` can contain `[T, T]` and still pass `evaluate_catalogue_lint`, violating AC-02/CN-03 and admitting an invalid Rust declaration. Add uniqueness validation and a rejection test.

The alias generic list is never validated for duplicate parameter names. `TypeAlias` can contain `[T, T]`, and the added linter paths only scan bounds, so `evaluate_catalogue_lint` can return success instead of the `DuplicateTypeAliasGenericParameter` validation error required by AC-02/CN-03 and T002. Add uniqueness validation and a rejection test.

Duplicate alias-generic validation only runs for `target_layer_id` (line 645), so aliases with duplicate parameter names in other catalogues in `all_catalogues` are accepted during evaluation. Validate every catalogue before delegating to the rule evaluator; otherwise the invariant depends on which layer happens to be reviewed.

The reserved-keyword list omits `gen`, which is a reserved keyword in Rust edition 2024. `ParamName::new("gen")` therefore succeeds, allowing generated generic/function declarations that fail to compile.

`ParamName` now rejects all Rust keywords even though raw identifiers are valid parameter/type-parameter names and rustdoc removes their `r#` prefix. Thus valid code such as `type Alias<r#type> = r#type;` reaches the catalogue as parameter name `type` and is rejected here, causing false catalogue/implementation mismatches. This normalization is already documented in `catalogue.rs:42-44`. Preserve rustdoc-normalized keyword names in the shared `ParamName`; enforce alias-generic-specific restrictions at that declaration boundary.

Valid raw generic identifiers are rejected after rustdoc normalization. Rustdoc strips `r#`, so `type Alias<r#type> = r#type;` reaches the catalogue with parameter name `type`; this blacklist then returns `InvalidTypeAliasGenericParameterName`, preventing a valid alias from linting or matching its implementation. Preserve normalized keyword names (while still rejecting `_`, duplicates, and malformed bounds), or retain raw-identifier provenance.

The validator accepts `self`, `Self`, `super`, and `crate`, but Rust forbids these spellings even as raw identifiers (`r#self`, etc.). A catalogue alias using any of them therefore passes lint validation despite having no valid Rust declaration. Reject these four names in addition to `_`, while continuing to accept keywords that can be raw identifiers, and add a regression test.

The keyword boundary is incomplete: Rust's weak keywords `macro_rules`, `raw`, and `safe` are omitted even though `union` is rejected. Because all three satisfy `ParamName`'s character rules, aliases using them pass validation despite AC-02 requiring plain non-keyword parameter names. Reject these remaining weak-keyword spellings and cover them in the keyword regression test.

The new alias-bound validation routes every bound through `PrimitiveOccurrenceScanner::scan(..., Bound)`, but this port parses a `TypeRef` as a type and does not accept valid `TypeParamBound`-only syntax. The same file documents that `?Sized` and lifetime bounds are legal catalogue bounds yet can fail this scanner (`BoundOnlyFailingScanner`), so a valid alias such as `type Alias<T: ?Sized> = ...` is rejected before rule evaluation with `ScanFailed`. Validate bound syntax with a bound-aware boundary or only reject the explicitly malformed/blank forms, while preserving valid bounds.

The replacement bound validation only rejects blank strings and bounds whose trimmed text starts with `<`; malformed bounds such as `!!!`, `T +`, `Vec<`, or `A::` remain accepted and reach rule evaluation. Since `TypeRef::new` intentionally permits these raw strings, this leaves the required catalogue-lint boundary unable to reject malformed alias bounds. The check needs a complete bound-aware syntax validation (or equivalent fail-closed validation), not two lexical cases.

When kind-level `generics` is non-empty, the fallback silently ignores `entry.generics()`. A programmatically constructed alias can therefore populate both declarations and bypass name, duplicate, and bound validation for the legacy list, even though the codec/encoder treats this dual-populated state as invalid and rule collectors may still inspect both lists. Reject the dual-populated case before selecting the legacy fallback and add regression coverage.

T001 is not executable: it names only abstract boundaries ("alias catalogue contract" / "strict serialization boundary"), not a target file or symbol, so the executor must invent the implementation boundary.
T002 is not executable: "catalogue linting" does not identify a target file or symbol, leaving the implementation boundary unspecified.
T003 is not executable: "catalogue-to-implementation lexical alias comparison" identifies a subsystem but no target file or symbol, so the executor must invent the boundary.
T004 is not executable: it requests a compatibility regression but names neither the target test file nor the comparison symbol.

T001 restates upstream behavior (preserving omitted declarations and adding malformed-declaration/read-write behavior) instead of using only target + operation + anchor. Remove the contract prose and retain an anchored operation per .harness/policies/no-upstream-restatement.md.
T002 restates AC-01/AC-02/CN-01 behavior (valid declarations pass, invalid declarations error, undeclared aliases retain their result) in the task text. Keep only the target, operation, and anchors.

T003 restates the comparison contract and out-of-scope boundaries (canonical spelling, matching/mismatch behavior, semantic parsing exclusion, and non-alias exclusion) in prose. Keep only the target, operation, and anchors.
T004 restates AC-05/CN-01 compatibility behavior (unchanged pre-extension result) in prose. Keep only the target, operation, and anchors.

Section S1 restates upstream behavior (optional declaration, validation, and preserving undeclared aliases) in its description. Section descriptions must avoid reproducing the spec contract; retain a concise plan label plus anchors.

Section S2 restates upstream behavior and boundaries (lexical comparison, existing boundary, and compatibility preservation) in its description. Remove the contract prose and retain only plan-level operation/anchors.

T001 is attributed to the catalogue entry `TypeKindV2`, but the current type catalogues are empty and the task description names `TypeKindV2` as an implementation symbol, not an existing catalogue entry. Remove this attribution (or attribute only a real catalogue entry); the empty-catalogue track must keep `entries` empty.

T001 still attributes the catalogue entry `TypeKindV2`, but the current catalogues are empty and the task description names `TypeKindV2` as an implementation symbol rather than an existing catalogue entry. Remove this attribution so the empty-catalogue track keeps `entries` empty.

AC-01 is mapped only to T001 and T002, which cover codec and lint behavior. AC-01 also requires legacy aliases without parameter declarations to retain their evaluation result; T004 is the only evaluator regression task, but it is omitted from this mapping and does not cite AC-01. Add T004 to AC-01 traceability or add equivalent evaluation validation to a mapped task.

T002 is estimated only in `infrastructure`, but its declared production target, `catalogue_linter::evaluate_catalogue_lint`, and associated tests are in `libs/domain`. Consequently B-01 omits T002's domain contribution, so admission cannot apply the domain ceiling when starting this task. Record T002's estimate under `domain` and retain an infrastructure estimate only if explicit infrastructure work is added to the task.

T002's batch estimate assigns all work to the `domain` scope, but the task targets `catalogue_linter::evaluate_catalogue_lint` and alias-entry fixtures, an infrastructure/catalogue-processing boundary. The declared estimate omits the scope where the described implementation and tests will land; restore the infrastructure estimate or revise the task target if it is genuinely domain-owned.

T002's task-contract attribution adds `domain / CatalogueLinterError`, but T002's description only names `catalogue_linter::evaluate_catalogue_lint` and test fixtures and does not identify any operation on `CatalogueLinterError`. An executor could implement the linter validation without the attributed catalogue entry, leaving the attribution unsupported.

T002's task-contract attribution includes `domain::tddd::catalogue_linter::eval::evaluate_catalogue_lint`, whose catalogue action is `delete`, but the task description names only `catalogue_linter::evaluate_catalogue_lint` and does not specify deleting or updating the `eval` implementation. The attributed internal function boundary is therefore not executable from T002's description.

Generic parameters decoded into `TypeKindV2::TypeAlias` are dropped during extended-crate encoding: this call passes only `target`, while `encode_type_alias` builds rustdoc generics from `entry.generics()` (the separate type-entry field). For the new wire shape, `entry.generics()` remains empty, so `type Foo<T> = ...` is encoded without `T` and structural comparison reports a mismatch instead of matching the implementation.

Type aliases still use the name-independent, normalized `generics_structurally_equal`. It canonicalizes parameter names and sorts bounds, so lexically different declarations can compare equal—for example `<T: Clone, U: Clone> = (T, U)` versus `<U: Clone, T: Clone> = (T, U)`, or `T: Clone + Send` versus `T: Send + Clone`. The added tests avoid these counterexamples. Use an alias-specific comparison that preserves parameter order, names, and bound spelling as required by CN-03.

The JSON DTO accepts both entry-level `generics` and alias-kind `generics`, but this selection silently discards the entry-level declaration whenever the alias-kind list is non-empty, while still applying entry-level `where_predicates`. A document containing conflicting declarations therefore decodes and round-trips but chain-③ evaluates only one of them. Reject conflicting dual declarations at the boundary or represent a single authoritative source.

Decode rejects duplicate alias generic names, but encode copies the public `Vec<MethodGenericParam>` without the equivalent validation. Consequently `CatalogueDocumentCodec::encode` can successfully emit JSON that the same codec refuses to decode. Make alias conversion fallible and return `InvalidEntry`, or enforce uniqueness in a validated domain collection.

Alias bound comparison strips qualified trait paths to their final segment (`foo::Trait` and `bar::Trait` both become `Trait`). This can mark semantically/lexically different alias declarations as equal, contrary to the required lexical bound comparison; preserve the full bound spelling (including qualified paths and nested argument paths).

Alias bound comparison still formats generic arguments with the shared short-name formatter. Thus bounds such as `Trait<foo::Arg>` and `Trait<bar::Arg>` can compare equal because nested paths are reduced to `Arg`, violating lexical bound comparison.

Non-parameter alias where-predicates are compared via `Debug`, which includes rustdoc path IDs. The A-side and implementation-side graphs use different IDs, so equivalent predicates containing resolved paths can compare unequal and produce false mismatches.

`type_kind_to_dto` validates duplicate names only in the new kind-level list. It serializes those bounds without `validate_bound_str`, and when that list is empty it does not validate the supported legacy `entry_generics` list at all. An in-memory alias with a malformed bound—or legacy generics `[T, T]`—therefore encodes successfully, while `method_generics_from_dtos` rejects the emitted JSON on decode. Validate the effective alias declaration with the same bound and uniqueness rules before emitting it.

Generic-name validation still accepts the reserved identifier `_`: `ParamName::new("_")` succeeds, so an alias with `generics: [{"name":"_","bounds":[]}]` crosses the document boundary even though Rust rejects `type Alias<_> = ...`. Reject `_` specifically for generic parameters and add a regression test.

Reserved keywords are still accepted. `ParamName::new` only validates identifier characters, so `ParamName::new("type")` succeeds and this error mapping is never entered. Consequently the new test at `mod.rs:889` panics and invalid Rust generic declarations still cross the document boundary. Add an explicit keyword check before constructing the generic parameter.

The new `_` rejection is decode-only. A domain alias can still contain `ParamName::new("_")`, and the encoder validates only duplicate names and bounds, so `encode` returns JSON that this branch immediately rejects on `decode`. Mirror generic-name validation in the encoding path and cover the encode error/round-trip behavior.

Keyword/wildcard validation is added to the shared decoder for every generic declaration, but encoding performs the equivalent validation only for type aliases. Consequently, domain values such as a function, trait, method, or impl with `ParamName::new("type")` or `ParamName::new("_")` encode successfully and then fail to decode, violating codec round-trip symmetry. Either restrict this new check to aliases or validate every generic-bearing encoder path.

This production-only module is now 713 lines, exceeding the repository's hard 700-line module limit. The newly added alias-name helper is also redundant with the validation already performed by `method_generics_from_dtos`; remove it or extract validation/conversion into a smaller module.

This production-only module is now 706 lines, exceeding the repository's hard 700-line module limit. Extract the newly added alias-name validation helper (for example into `validate.rs`) or otherwise reduce the module below the limit.

Accepting rustdoc-normalized keywords here does not preserve enough information for extended-crate encoding. For valid `type Alias<r#type> = Vec<r#type>;`, the parameter becomes `type`; `Vec<type>` cannot be parsed by `syn`, while `Vec<r#type>` yields `r#type`, which does not match the stored generic name and is not encoded as `Type::Generic`. The false mismatch therefore remains whenever the raw parameter is referenced. Normalize raw identifiers during generic matching (or retain raw provenance) and add an end-to-end regression test.

The raw-keyword normalization is token-blind: when a declared generic is named `for` (from source `r#for`), a valid target such as `for<'a> fn(&'a str)` has its syntactic `for` rewritten to `r#for` and then fails `syn` parsing; the same collision affects syntax keywords such as `dyn`, `impl`, and `fn`. Restrict restoration to identifier-reference positions (or preserve raw-identifier provenance) and add collision tests.

This edit pushes the production module from 699 to 702 lines, exceeding the repository's 700-line maximum; `bin/sotp verify module-size` reports this file as an error. Split or move helpers (or otherwise reduce the production module) so the structural gate passes.

Accepting rustdoc-normalized keyword names here is still inconsistent with document-boundary syntax validation. A valid alias such as `type Alias<r#type, U: Into<r#type>> = ...` produces the normalized bound `Into<type>`, but decode and encode pass that directly to `validate_bound_str`, so `syn` rejects it before the generic-aware parser can restore `r#`. Make alias bound/where-predicate validation aware of the declared generic names and add round-trip coverage.

The syntax-position heuristic assumes `dyn` and `impl` syntax must be followed by an ASCII identifier, but Rust paths may start with `::`. With generic `dyn`, the valid normalized target `dyn ::Trait<dyn>` fails its direct parse at the inner reference; fallback then prefixes both tokens because the first is followed by `:`, producing `r#dyn::Trait<r#dyn>` and encoding a path instead of `Type::DynTrait`. Recognize the complete path grammar, including leading `::`, and add an end-to-end mixed-keyword test.

Accepting rustdoc-normalized keyword names here is still inconsistent with document-boundary syntax validation. A valid alias such as `type Alias<r#type, U: Into<r#type>> = ...` produces the normalized bound `Into<type>`, but decode and encode pass that directly to `validate_bound_str`, so `syn` rejects it before the generic-aware parser can restore `r#`. Make alias bound/where-predicate validation aware of the declared generic names and add round-trip coverage.

The syntax-position heuristic still assumes `dyn`/`impl` is followed immediately by a type path, but a valid bound list may begin with a lifetime. With generic `dyn`, normalized `dyn 'static + Trait<dyn>` fails direct parsing at the inner reference; fallback then rewrites the leading `dyn` too because the next token is `'`, so the valid source form `dyn 'static + Trait<r#dyn>` is rejected. Recognize the full trait-bound grammar and add this mixed lifetime/keyword case end-to-end.
現時点で、対象内の `decode.rs` が production 712 行となり、リポジトリの 700 行上限チェックに失敗することを確認しました。残りの差分について correctness の再判定を続けています。

Generic alias targets containing associated-type projections are misencoded. For example, `type Alias<T: Iterator> = T::Item` reaches this multi-segment branch before `generic_params` are consulted, registers `T` as an external crate, and emits `ResolvedPath("T::Item")`; rustdoc emits a `QualifiedPath` whose self type is `Generic("T")`, causing a false structural-equality mismatch. Recognize declared-generic prefixes as projections before external-crate or keyword-syntax parsing and add a target regression test.

Keyword-named generic projections can still be parsed using the wrong grammar. For example, an alias declared as `type Alias<r#dyn: Iterator> = r#dyn::Item` is represented in the catalogue as `dyn::Item`, but the initial parse succeeds as trait-object syntax, so normalization and the generic-projection branch are skipped. The A-side emits `DynTrait` instead of rustdoc's `QualifiedPath` over `Generic("dyn")`, causing a false structural mismatch. Disambiguate declared-generic projection prefixes before accepting the direct parse and add a regression test.

A declared raw generic named `dyn` cannot be used in an associated-type projection. Rustdoc normalizes `r#dyn::Item` to `dyn::Item`, but `syn::parse_str` accepts that text as `dyn ::Item` trait-object syntax, so the fallback never restores `r#`. The codec then emits a `DynTrait` instead of `QualifiedPath { self_type: Generic("dyn"), ... }`, breaking structural comparison for the alias. Handle normalized generic projections before accepting the direct parse (the same ambiguity applies to `impl`).

`normalize_generic_identifier_spelling` treats every otherwise-unhandled keyword occurrence as a generic reference. For a generic named `const`, the valid rustdoc-normalized target `*const const` (source: `*const r#const`) becomes `*r#const r#const`; the fallback original is also unparseable, so a valid alias is rejected. Distinguish pointer/reference modifiers such as `const` and `mut` from raw generic references.

Generic-aware validation now accepts nested keyword-generic references in alias where predicates, but the downstream extended-crate encoder parses non-bare where-clause LHS/RHS without passing the generic context. For example, an alias declaring generic `type` with LHS `Vec<type>` decodes successfully here but later fails `CatalogueToExtendedCrateCodec::encode`. Thread the alias generic names through where-form type parsing or keep this boundary fail-closed.

Keyword normalization mishandles qualified paths for keyword-named alias generics. For example, `<as as Trait>::Assoc` (source `<r#as as Trait>::Assoc`) becomes `<r#as r#as Trait>::Assoc`; the original spelling is also unparsable, so the extended-crate adapter rejects a valid alias. `dyn` and `impl` similarly remain syntax when used as the qself type before `as`. Preserve the qualified-path `as` delimiter while restoring the qself identifier.

The scanner treats every `"` as a normal-string boundary and does not honor raw-string delimiters. With a generic named `type`, a valid normalized target such as `(type, Foo<{ r#"x " type"#.len() }>)` is transformed to one whose raw-string contents contain `r#type`. The normalized form remains valid Rust, so fallback never occurs and the const-generic value is silently changed. Raw and byte-raw literals must be copied according to their complete hash-delimited token.

Unhandled keywords default to generic-identifier rewriting even inside const-generic expressions. For example, normalized `(if, Foo<{ if true { 1 } else { 2 } }>)` for `type Alias<r#if>` rewrites both `if` tokens; the normalized form is invalid and the original cannot parse because of the bare generic reference, so a valid alias is rejected. Keyword restoration must distinguish embedded expression syntax from type-identifier positions.

Qualified-path detection remains limited to direct `<dyn as ...>`/`<impl as ...>` heads and a small set of preceding delimiter characters. A valid target such as `<*const dyn as Trait>::Assoc` (source `<*const r#dyn as Trait>::Assoc`) leaves `dyn` as syntax because it is not immediately after `<`, causing both parse attempts to fail. The `as` delimiter is likewise rewritten when the qself type ends in an unrecognized valid token such as `!`. Handle the complete qself type rather than relying on adjacent-character heuristics.

Every apostrophe is probed as a character literal, and `char_literal_end` accepts arbitrary content through the next apostrophe. In `for<'a> fn(type, &'a str)` with alias generic `type`, the first lifetime therefore swallows `type` through the second lifetime marker, so it is never restored to `r#type`; both parse attempts reject the otherwise valid alias. Distinguish lifetime tokens from actual one-character/escaped character literals.

The normalizer copies entire braced const expressions without restoring any raw identifiers. A valid normalized target such as `(type, Foo<{ let type = 1; type }>)` for `type Alias<r#type>` requires the outer generic and the raw const-expression identifiers to regain `r#`; only the outer occurrence is repaired, leaving invalid expression syntax, while fallback fails on the outer bare keyword. Const-expression syntax must be tokenized rather than skipped wholesale.

Any `dyn` before a qualified path's `as` delimiter is now classified as a raw generic occurrence. This breaks genuine trait-object qself syntax when an alias also declares a generic named `dyn`: `(dyn, <dyn Trait as Foo>::Assoc)` should normalize only the first occurrence, but becomes `(r#dyn, <r#dyn Trait as Foo>::Assoc)` and is rejected. Require the qself occurrence itself to have generic-reference shape instead of treating every pre-delimiter `dyn` as generic.

Unhandled expression keywords default to raw-identifier rewriting. With alias generic `true`, normalized `(true, Foo<{ if true { 1 } else { 2 } }>)` becomes `(r#true, Foo<{ if r#true { 1 } else { 2 } }>)`. This still parses, so fallback never runs and the boolean literal is silently encoded as an identifier expression, changing the const-generic semantics. Expression syntax such as `true`, `false`, casts, and other keywords must be distinguished from raw identifiers.

The qself classifier treats any following `:` as evidence that `dyn` is a raw generic projection, even when whitespace makes it genuine trait-object syntax. Thus `(dyn, <dyn ::core::fmt::Debug as Foo>::Assoc)` for generic `dyn` normalizes the second occurrence to `r#dyn`, and both parse attempts reject a valid alias. Preserve spaced `dyn ::Trait` syntax inside qualified paths just as the non-qself branch does.

Production code now runs through line 727 before the `#[cfg(test)]` block, exceeding the repository's 700-line maximum for production modules. Split the normalization/lexical helpers into a focused sibling module so this infrastructure module conforms to the architecture guideline.

`is_const_expr_identifier_position` treats every unlisted keyword inside a const expression as a generic identifier. For example, the valid alias `type Alias<r#as> = (r#as, Foo<{ 1 as usize }>);` is normalized from `(as, Foo<{ 1 as usize }>)` to `(r#as, Foo<{ 1 r#as usize }>)`. The normalized parse then fails, while fallback parsing fails on the outer `as`, so extended-crate encoding rejects a valid generic alias. Const-expression syntax keywords need context-aware preservation instead of the catch-all branch.

The const-expression classifier does not recognize numeric literals as expression starts. For the valid alias `type Alias<r#if> = (r#if, Foo<{ if 1 == 1 { 1 } else { 2 } }>);`, the rustdoc-normalized target causes the inner syntax keyword `if` to be rewritten as `r#if`. The normalized parse then fails, while fallback parsing fails on the outer normalized generic name, so the adapter rejects a valid alias.

Precise-capture `use<...>` syntax is not exempted from keyword restoration. For valid code such as `fn f<r#use>() -> impl Sized + use<r#use>`, the normalized return type `impl Sized + use<use>` becomes `impl Sized + r#use<r#use>`. `syn` accepts this as an ordinary trait bound, so the adapter silently emits a trait named `use` instead of the capture bound, corrupting the extended-crate structure.

`convert_impl_trait` silently drops `syn::TypeParamBound::PreciseCapture`. After the new normalizer makes rustdoc-normalized `impl Sized + use<use>` parse as `use<r#use>`, the encoded `Type::ImplTrait` loses that capture bound instead of emitting the available `GenericBound::Use`, causing structural drift from rustdoc output.

The const-expression keyword heuristic corrupts valid raw identifiers. The `in` arm is inverted: a loop separator followed by an expression is marked as an identifier, while `let r#in = 1; r#in` in rustdoc-normalized form is left unescaped and rejected. Nearby hard-coded cases also misclassify raw `true`/`false` locals and patterned `let` syntax, so accepted keyword generic names cannot reliably round-trip through const-generic expressions.

`const_expr_locals` makes every later token with the same spelling a raw identifier, even when it is Rust syntax. For valid `type Alias<r#true> = (r#true, Foo<{ let r#true = 1; if true { r#true } else { 0 } }>);`, the boolean literal in `if true` becomes `r#true`; the normalized form still parses, so the codec silently changes the const expression instead of falling back.

The `let` classifier recognizes only a single identifier immediately followed by `=`. With a declared generic named `let`, valid syntax such as `let mut x = 1` or `let (x, y) = ...` is therefore rewritten to `r#let`, causing otherwise valid rustdoc-normalized alias targets to be rejected.

The newly expanded `parse_ctx.rs` is 721 production lines and has no test-only section to exclude, exceeding the repository's explicit 700-line maximum. Move the precise-capture or generic-argument conversion helpers into a sibling module.

The local-binding state does not make keyword occurrence classification lossless. It is ignored for control/cast keywords, so valid `let r#if = 1; r#if + 1` leaves the reference unescaped; conversely it forces later `let` syntax and parenthesized boolean literals to raw identifiers, corrupting cases such as `let r#let = 1; let x = 2` and `if (true)`. These valid inputs are rejected or silently converted to a different const-expression AST.

`collect_let_binding_names` treats every keyword-looking token in a pattern as a binding, including pattern modifiers. With an alias generic named `mut`, ordinary valid syntax `let mut x = 1` records `mut` as a local and is rewritten to invalid `let r#mut x = 1`; `ref` and keyword literal patterns have the same problem. Pattern bindings must be distinguished from modifiers and literals.

Local bindings are ignored for control-flow-shaped keywords. For valid Rust such as `type A<r#if> = (r#if, Foo<{ let r#if = 1; r#if + 1 }>);`, normalized input contains `let if = 1; if + 1`. The declaration is restored, but the reference is treated as `if` syntax because `+` counts as a condition start. The normalized parse fails, while fallback cannot parse the outer keyword generic, so the valid catalogue is rejected.

The binding-pattern blacklist makes valid raw keyword bindings unrecoverable. For example, `let r#mut = 1` normalizes to `let mut = 1`, but `mut` is forcibly treated as syntax and is not recorded as a local. An alias using both a generic and local named `r#mut` therefore fails both normalized and fallback parsing. Pattern modifiers must be distinguished by grammar position rather than a fixed name blacklist.

Once a local named `r#let` is recorded, every subsequent `let` token is classified as an identifier. In valid code such as `type A<r#let> = (r#let, Foo<{ let r#let = 1; let x = 2; r#let + x }>);`, the second declaration is rewritten from syntax to `r#let x = 2`, making parsing fail. Local-name tracking must not override an occurrence that has the grammar of a `let` statement.

Multi-level generic projections silently lose their intermediate segments. Valid Rust such as `type X<T> where T: Outer = T::Assoc::Nested` enters this branch, but only the first and last segments are retained, yielding a projection equivalent to `T::Nested`. This corrupts the extended-crate representation and breaks structural comparison with rustdoc.

The `let` pattern scanner treats the first top-level `=` byte as an assignment without distinguishing operators such as `==`. For a valid normalized expression originating from `let r#let = 1; r#let == 1`, the reference `let == 1` is misclassified as a new `let` expression and is not restored to `r#let`, causing the valid alias target to fail parsing.

`is_binding_pattern_modifier` accepts any following non-whitespace character because `next_identifier_end` advances even when started on punctuation. Consequently, a valid normalized tuple pattern such as `let (mut, x) = ...`, originating from `let (r#mut, x)`, treats `mut` as a modifier because it is followed by `,`; the raw binding is not restored or recorded and the valid catalogue is rejected.

Boolean keyword spellings are unconditionally treated as literal patterns, although Rust permits raw bindings named `r#true` and `r#false`. A valid alias such as `type A<r#true> = (r#true, Foo<{ let r#true = 1; r#true + 1 }>);` is normalized into literal-pattern/literal-expression syntax instead of restoring the local identifier. Because this remains syntactically parseable, the codec can silently emit a semantically different const expression.

Control-keyword classification still ignores the recorded local binding and relies only on the next character. For example, valid `let r#if = 2; r#if - 1` normalizes to `let if = 2; if - 1`; since `-` is considered a condition start, the reference is left as `if` syntax and parsing fails. The same issue affects other handled control/cast keywords followed by operators that can also begin expressions.

Inside const-expression braces, every keyword not explicitly listed in this match is assumed to be a raw identifier. This corrupts genuine syntax when an alias generic has the same normalized name: for example, with a generic `r#return`, the `return` statement in `Foo<{ const fn f() -> usize { return 1; } f() }>` is rewritten to `r#return`, so valid Rust is rejected. Other unhandled expression/item keywords such as `fn`, `const`, `unsafe`, and `async` have the same failure mode.

The `let` pattern scanner does not stop at a statement boundary and still mistakes compound operators whose `=` is the second character for an assignment. For valid `let r#let = 1; r#let + 1; let x = 2; x`, the normalized reference `let + 1` scans through the semicolon to the later `=`, is classified as `let` syntax, and is not restored. Expressions such as `r#let != 2` fail similarly.

Boolean raw bindings are inferred from the initializer spelling, which cannot distinguish `let true = true` originating from a literal pattern versus `let r#true = true`. A valid alias using `let mut r#true = true; r#true = false` is classified as boolean literals, so its bindings and references are not restored and the codec parses a semantically different expression.

The local-binding operator exception omits `*` and `&`, although both can follow a raw local in ordinary binary expressions. Valid `let r#if = 2; r#if * 2` therefore leaves the normalized reference as `if * 2`, treating it as a control-flow head and rejecting the alias. The same defect affects the other control/cast keyword branches using this helper.

With a generic named `true`, valid input such as `(true, [u8; { match 0 { /* true */ _ => 1 } }])` is rejected because `pattern_contains_boolean_literal` treats `true` inside the comment as an arm pattern. Skip line and nested block comments throughout the match scanner before inspecting tokens or delimiters.

Keyword-position lookahead ignores comments, so comment-separated syntax keywords are rewritten as generic identifiers. For example, with generic `dyn`, `dyn /* comment */ Trait<dyn>` becomes `r#dyn /* comment */ Trait<r#dyn>` and fails parsing; the fallback also fails on the normalized inner generic, rejecting the valid source-equivalent `dyn /* comment */ Trait<r#dyn>`. Make the lookahead and main normalizer treat comments as opaque whitespace.

The main identifier normalizer still does not treat comments as opaque, even though the new helper scanners do. Comment delimiters therefore mutate its brace/array/parenthesis state: with generic `dyn`, valid normalized input `/* { */ dyn Trait<dyn>` (source-equivalent to `/* { */ dyn Trait<r#dyn>`) enters const-expression mode from the brace inside the comment and rewrites the syntax `dyn`, causing parsing to fail. Copy comments wholesale with `comment_end` before updating lexical state or inspecting identifiers.

The fail-closed boolean-ambiguity check can be bypassed when a comment separates a type path from its generic arguments. For generic `true`, `Foo /* comment */ <true>` makes `looks_like_generic_open` see the comment terminator `/` instead of `Foo`, so ambiguity validation passes and normalization silently converts the possible boolean const argument into `Foo<r#true>`/`Type::Generic`. Make the generic-open and close delimiter checks skip comments as well as whitespace.

The ambiguity scan treats every top-level `true`/`false` token inside angle brackets as a boolean argument, including associated-item bindings such as `dyn Trait<true = u8>`. When an alias generic is named `true`, this valid spelling could be losslessly normalized to `r#true`, but validation rejects it before normalization. Inspect the token's syntactic role and only reject standalone ambiguous boolean arguments.

The generic-close delimiter list excludes `(`. Consequently, an alias target such as `[u8; core::mem::size_of::<true>()]` with generic `true` bypasses ambiguity validation; const-expression normalization then preserves `true` as a boolean literal, silently changing the intended `::<r#true>()` type argument. Recognize turbofish call continuations or otherwise validate the argument role before accepting it.

Pointer/reference modifier detection skips whitespace but not comments. For a generic named `const`, normalized input `* /* comment */ const const` should become `* /* comment */ const r#const`; instead the first `const` is misclassified and rawified too, causing a valid type to be rejected. Determine the preceding syntactic token while treating comments as trivia.

The boolean-argument ambiguity check exempts associated equality bindings ending in `=`, but not associated bound constraints ending in `:`. With an alias generic named `true`, the valid normalized target `dyn Trait<true: Send>` can be losslessly restored to `dyn Trait<r#true: Send>`, yet it is rejected as an ambiguous boolean argument. Exempt syntactically named associated constraints as well as equality bindings.

The generic-close delimiter list still excludes `{`. A const expression such as `S::<true> { value: 0 }` therefore bypasses fail-closed ambiguity detection when `true` is an alias generic; normalization leaves it as a boolean const argument instead of detecting the possible `::<r#true>` type argument. Recognize struct-literal continuations after turbofish generic lists.

Binding-pattern modifier detection skips whitespace but not comments. For a generic named `mut`, the valid normalized target `[mut; { let mut /* comment */ value = 0; 1 }]` is transformed into an invalid `let r#mut ... value` pattern; the original fallback also cannot parse the unraw element type, so the adapter rejects a valid alias. Treat comments as trivia when locating the identifier following `mut`/`ref`/`box`.

The `for`-pattern boundary scan does not skip comments, so an `in` token inside a comment terminates the pattern early. For an alias generic named `true`, `[true; { for /* in */ true in 0..1 {} 1 }]` then bypasses the boolean-binding ambiguity gate and is parsed with `true` as a literal pattern rather than the normalized `r#true` binding. Make comments opaque while locating the real `in` separator.

`next_identifier` skips whitespace but not comments. In an alias target such as `[true; { const fn /* comment */ f(true: usize) { } 0 }]` with generic `true`, the normalizer cannot recognize `fn` as syntax and rewrites it to `r#fn`; the normalized parse then fails, while the original fallback cannot parse the unraw element type. Treat comments as trivia in identifier lookahead.

`macro_invocation_end` counts delimiters inside comments. For `[u8; m!(/* ) */ Foo<true>)]` with generic `true`, it ends the opaque macro at the commented `)`, after which the ambiguity scanner examines `Foo<true>` and rejects an invocation that should remain opaque. Skip comments while matching macro delimiters.

Binding-scope delimiter matching does not skip comments. A parameter list such as `const fn f(/* ) */ true: usize)` is truncated at the commented `)`, so a boolean-named generic binding bypasses ambiguity validation and is interpreted as a literal pattern. The same issue affects brace-based and closure-body scope tracking. Make comments opaque in the delimiter walkers.

`collect_let_binding_names` scans identifiers inside comments. With generic `return`, `[return; { const fn f() { let /* return */ x = 0; return; } 0 }]` falsely records a local named `return`, causing the real control-flow keyword to be rewritten as `r#return` and silently changing the parsed expression. Skip comments before collecting binding names.

Comment-separated syntax is still misclassified because this lookahead skips only whitespace. For example, an alias target equivalent to `[r#loop; { loop /* comment */ {} }]` is normalized from `[loop; { loop /* comment */ {} }]` by changing the loop-expression keyword to `r#loop`; the normalized parse fails, while the original spelling cannot parse the generic element type. Valid keyword-generic aliases containing comments are therefore rejected. Make this shared lookahead skip comments as well as whitespace.

`item_binding_name` treats the first `/` of a comment as the item name. With a target such as `[if; { const fn /* comment */ if() -> usize { 1 } if() }]`, the keyword-named function is not registered as a local binding, so its declaration/call is not restored to `r#if` and the valid alias is rejected. Skip comments while locating the name after an item keyword.

The closure-parameter terminator scan does not treat comments or literals as opaque, so a `|` inside a comment prematurely closes the parameter list. A keyword-named parameter appearing afterward is then omitted from the closure scope; for example, the body call in `|x /* | */, fn: fn()| fn()` remains `fn()` instead of `r#fn()`, rejecting or changing a valid normalized alias target.

Conditional-let scope detection is not comment-aware: `previous_identifier` cannot recognize `if /* comment */ let`, and the subsequent body scan also counts braces inside comments. The binding is consequently promoted to the entire const-expression scope or given the wrong end, which can rawify later syntax—for example, a local `r#fn` from the conditional can cause a following `type X = fn()` to become `type X = r#fn()`. This rejects or semantically changes valid alias targets.

The boolean-parameter ambiguity scanner interprets delimiters inside comments. In `fn f(/* : */ true: usize)`, the colon in the comment terminates `parameter_segment_contains_boolean` before the normalized `true` parameter, so the required fail-closed ambiguity error is bypassed and the parser can silently treat the raw identifier as a boolean literal pattern. Both parameter-segmentation loops need comment/literal skipping.

The generic-close whitelist omits valid expression continuations such as the `as` cast keyword and several operators. Thus a normalized ambiguous argument in `f::<true> as fn()` is not examined when `true` is also a declared generic name; the adapter silently encodes it as the boolean const argument even when the source used the type argument `r#true`. Determine generic closure from Rust token context or include all valid continuations so the ambiguity gate remains fail-closed.

The `fn` rule only preserves a named function item when the name is immediately followed by a parenthesis group. A valid nested item such as `fn f<T>() {}` has `<` after the name, so with a generic named `fn` the syntax keyword is rewritten to `r#fn`. An alias target such as `(fn, [u8; { fn f<T>() {} 0 }])` is therefore rejected even though its raw-identifier source is valid.

`mut`, `ref`, and `box` are preserved as modifiers only when the immediately preceding token is `let`. This rewrites ordinary type/pattern modifiers: for example, normalized `&mut mut` for `type Alias<r#mut> = &mut r#mut` becomes `&r#mut r#mut` and cannot parse. Modifier detection must cover reference and nested-pattern grammar, not just `let mut`.

The `as` rule rewrites every ordinary cast delimiter because the preceding token is normally the expression, not another `as`. With a declared generic named `as`, a target containing both the generic type and an unrelated `0 as usize` cast changes the cast keyword to `r#as`, making a valid alias fail parsing. The cast delimiter needs to be recognized from its syntactic position.

Several control-flow keyword rules recognize only one narrow following-token shape. For example, `if (condition)` is rewritten because the condition is a parenthesis group, `else if` is rewritten because `if` is not a brace group, and `return 0`/`break 1` are rewritten because they are not immediately followed by `;`. When the alias declares the corresponding keyword generic, these valid constructs inside const expressions become invalid raw-identifier expressions.

The `in` separator is preserved only when its immediately preceding token is `for`, but every real `for` loop has a pattern between those tokens. Consequently, with a generic named `in`, even `for _ in 0..1` is normalized to `for _ r#in 0..1`. Valid alias targets containing a loop—such as one inside a nested function in a const block—are rejected.

Unhandled keywords are always restored as raw identifiers, even when they are syntax. This silently changes a precise-capture bound such as `use<use>` (for a generic named `use`) into the syntactically valid trait path `r#use<r#use>`, so `GenericBound::Use` is encoded as `TraitBound`. It also rejects nested items such as `type X = u8` when `type` is a declared generic. Syntax keywords need contextual handling rather than the unconditional default.

Whitespace-separated absolute trait paths are repaired only when `dyn`/`impl` begins the entire input. In a nested type such as `Box<dyn ::Trait>`, `dyn` is rewritten to `r#dyn` when `dyn` is also a generic name, and the post-processing at the start of `normalize` does not restore it. The adapter then silently encodes a projection rooted at the generic instead of the intended trait object.

Boolean ambiguity validation rejects every normalized `true` or `false` token outside an associated binding, regardless of grammatical position. This rejects unambiguous supported declarations such as `type Alias<r#true> = r#true`, whose catalogue target is the bare type `true`; a boolean literal cannot occupy that top-level type position. The fail-closed check must distinguish genuinely ambiguous generic/const positions from type-only positions.

Nested methods are validated using only their method-level generics. For a trait/impl/type generic named `r#type`, a method predicate such as `Vec<type>: Clone` or a method-generic bound containing `type` is rejected because enclosing generic names are absent; decoding has the same omission. Combine enclosing and method generic contexts in both codec directions.

Trait generics are decoded after supertrait bounds and are not passed to associated-type/const decoders. Consequently, an encoded trait such as `trait Foo<r#type>: Super<r#type>` (or an associated item using that parameter) emits normalized `type` spellings that the decoder rejects, breaking encode/decode symmetry.

Boolean ambiguity validation exempts only an exact bare type. Unambiguous type-position uses such as `&'static true`, `fn(true)`, or `(true,)` are rejected whenever `true` is a declared raw generic, even though these positions cannot represent boolean expressions and can safely be restored to `r#true`.

The boolean scanner treats any declared boolean keyword followed by `=` inside angle brackets as an associated binding. In a valid const argument such as `Assert<{ true == false }>` with a generic named `r#true`, validation therefore passes and normalization rewrites the literal to `r#true`, silently changing the encoded type instead of failing closed.

The `const` classifier treats every occurrence following `&` as syntax, although references have no `const` modifier. A valid raw-generic type such as `fn(&r#const)` is normalized by rustdoc to `fn(&const)` and is left unescaped here, so both parse attempts fail.

Declared generics named `return`, `break`, or `continue` are restored only when directly followed by `:`. Ordinary references such as `Vec<return>` therefore remain keywords and cannot be parsed, rejecting valid aliases declared with `r#return` (and equivalently `r#break`/`r#continue`).

The `type` branch assumes any following identifier denotes a type-item declaration. This misclassifies qualified-self references: `<type as Trait>::Assoc` from an alias generic `r#type` is left unchanged and rejected by `syn`. Several other syntax-head branches have the same qself failure, so qself detection must precede keyword-specific classification.

A binding/reference modifier is recognized only when its next token is an identifier. In `&mut (mut,)` for a generic named `r#mut`, the first `mut` is valid modifier syntax but is followed by a parenthesized group, so it is rewritten to `r#mut`; the normalized form and the original normalized rustdoc spelling both fail to parse.

Whitespace-path restoration compares occurrence indexes from all source keyword tokens against indexes from only rewritten raw tokens. With `(dyn, Box<dyn Trait>, Box<dyn ::core::fmt::Debug>)`, the intervening unchanged `dyn Trait` shifts the source index, so the final trait-object `dyn` remains `r#dyn` and is encoded as a generic projection instead of a `DynTrait`.

The boolean ambiguity gate mistakes the `=` in a match fat arrow for an associated binding because it excludes `==` but not `=>`. With a declared generic named `true`, `(true, Foo<{ match FLAG { true => 1, false => 0 } }>)` passes validation and normalization changes the boolean pattern to the identifier binding `r#true`, silently altering semantics.

A comma is always classified as introducing a type position, even inside generic arguments where the following argument may be a const. For generic `true`, `(true, Foo<0, true>)` is accepted and normalized to `(r#true, Foo<0, r#true>)`, converting the boolean const argument into a type argument.

The ambiguity validator rejects `use<true>` when `true` is a declared raw generic, although a precise-capture argument is unambiguously an identifier or lifetime and the new precise-capture converter supports it. This prevents valid keyword-generic bounds from round-tripping.

`qself_type_identifier` does not require the candidate identifier to follow `<`; it marks any non-leading keyword with a later top-level `as` as a qself type. For example, with generic `if`, `(if, Foo<{ let flag = true; if flag as usize != 0 { 1 } else { 0 } }>)` rewrites the real `if` keyword to `r#if`, making the valid type unparseable.

Source occurrence counting ignores already-raw identifiers while output occurrence counting includes them. Mixed input such as `(r#dyn, dyn ::Trait<dyn>)` shifts the occurrence indexes, removes the user's first raw marker, and fails to restore the actual whitespace-sensitive `dyn` syntax occurrence, so a valid type cannot be parsed despite the API promise to preserve raw spellings.

Every declared-generic occurrence of `const` is rewritten unless preceded by `*`, including real const-item syntax. With generic `const`, `(const, Foo<{ const N: usize = 0; N }>)` rewrites both occurrences, making the nested item invalid; fallback parsing also fails on the normalized outer generic.

The control-flow syntax detector only recognizes a few operand shapes. Valid blocks such as `let (x, y) = ...`, `if !flag`, `match 0`, and `for (_, _) in values` have their syntax keywords rewritten when the same spelling is a declared generic, causing otherwise valid catalogue type references to be rejected.

This production module is 716 lines and has no test-only section, exceeding the repository's explicit 700-line maximum for production modules. The extraction into `decode_assoc.rs` and `decode_impls.rs` therefore does not yet satisfy the infrastructure architecture gate.

Resolve declared generics before primitive types. For `type Alias<r#bool> = r#bool`, rustdoc-normalized `bool` is returned as `Type::Primitive("bool")` before `generic_params` is consulted, while rustdoc emits `Type::Generic("bool")`; valid aliases using primitive-spelled generic names therefore fail structural equality.

Do not classify every angle-depth-zero boolean token as a type. With a declared `r#true` generic, normalized `(true, [u8; true as usize])` passes validation and the array-length literal is rewritten to `r#true`, changing the encoded constant expression instead of failing closed.

Exclude lifetime identifiers from raw-generic restoration. A valid declaration such as `type Alias<r#static: 'static> = r#static` rewrites the lifetime bound to `'r#static`; lifetime conversion then preserves that spelling instead of rustdoc's `'static`, causing a false structural mismatch.

Recognize nested block-item keywords before the default rawification branch. For a valid target such as `(r#static, [u8; { static N: usize = 1; N }])`, rustdoc normalization removes the first `r#`, after which this code also rewrites the item head to `r#static N`; normalized parsing fails and fallback parsing cannot parse the bare outer `static`, so a valid catalogue is rejected.

Seed duplicate detection with `outer_generic_names`. The decoder currently accepts an enclosing `T` and a nested method generic also named `T` (for example `trait Service<T> { fn run<T>(); }`), although Rust rejects this with E0403, allowing an impossible declaration through the adapter boundary.

Do not assume every keyword immediately after `<` in a qualified path is the generic qself identifier. With a generic named `r#fn` and target `(r#fn, <fn() as Marker>::Assoc)`, rustdoc-normalized input causes both `fn` tokens to be rawified; the normalized form is invalid while the original cannot parse the first bare `fn`, so a valid source declaration is rejected.

A valid qself whose self type begins with trait-object syntax is mistaken for a keyword-named generic. For example, with a generic named `dyn`, the rustdoc-normalized target `(dyn, <dyn Marker as Other>::Assoc)` needs only the first occurrence restored. `qself_type_identifier` also forces the second `dyn` to `r#dyn`, making the normalized qself invalid, while parsing the original fails on the actual generic occurrence. Valid aliases combining a `dyn` generic with a trait-object qself are therefore rejected.

The keyword-preservation rules omit legal block items such as `struct`, `enum`, `trait`, `mod`, and `use`. For example, rustdoc-normalized `type Alias<r#struct> = (r#struct, [u8; { struct S; 0 }]);` is rewritten with both occurrences as `r#struct`, corrupting the local item declaration. The normalized form is invalid and the original cannot parse because of the real generic occurrence, so valid catalogue input is rejected.

Boolean keyword generics in nested array or slice element position are incorrectly classified as ambiguous. For `Option<[r#true; 1]>`, rustdoc supplies `Option<[true; 1]>`; recursion enters the bracket group's contents at nonzero angle depth, but the opening bracket is no longer present as a token, so the `previous == '['` check can never recognize `true` as the element type. Validation rejects this valid alias before raw-identifier restoration can occur.

The qself syntax exemption for `dyn` only handles an identifier immediately after `dyn`. A valid lifetime-first trait object such as `type Alias<r#dyn> = (r#dyn, <dyn 'static + Marker as Other>::Assoc);` reaches this branch with `'` as the next token, so the qself occurrence is incorrectly restored to `r#dyn`. The normalized form is invalid, while parsing the original rustdoc spelling fails on the actual generic occurrence, causing a valid alias to be rejected.

Nested item heads are now preserved, but syntax within those items is still rewritten. For example, in the valid alias `type Alias<r#where> = (r#where, [u8; { fn f<T>() where T: Copy {} 0 }]);`, the outer `where` must become `r#where` while the function's `where` clause must remain syntax. The default branch rewrites both, making normalized parsing fail; fallback parsing also fails on the real generic occurrence. Valid catalogue targets containing nested items with keyword clauses or modifiers are therefore still rejected.

The array-length ambiguity scan loses its `in_length` state when it enters a nested group. Consequently, a valid source such as `type Alias<r#true> = (r#true, [u8; (true as usize)]);` is not rejected after rustdoc normalizes both occurrences to `true`: the parenthesized literal is missed by `contains_array_length_boolean`, then treated as a type-position occurrence and rewritten to `r#true`. This bypasses the intended fail-closed gate and changes the array-length expression instead of reporting the ambiguity.

The keyword restorer still rewrites valid syntax tokens that are not covered by the special cases. For example, with a generic named `async`, the valid target `(async, [u8; { async fn f() {} 0 }])` restores both occurrences to `r#async`; the nested item becomes invalid, while parsing the original also fails at the generic reference. Lifetime- or qself-leading nested `where` clauses have the same problem. Legitimate rustdoc-normalized aliases are therefore rejected.

Boolean ambiguity detection does not recognize all unambiguous type positions. For a generic named `true`, a valid target such as `Box<*const true>` is rejected because the pointee follows `const` rather than one of the predecessors checked here; `<true as Trait>::Assoc` is similarly rejected after `<`. These positions cannot contain boolean literals and should be normalized as raw type identifiers instead of failing closed.

The combined outer/method generic context is used to validate where predicates during encoding, but method generic bounds are still serialized through the infallible `method_generic_params_to_dtos`. The decoder now validates those bounds with the combined context, so an in-memory declaration such as generic `true` with bound `Marker<true>` encodes successfully and then cannot decode due to the ambiguity gate. Apply the same generic-aware validation on encode for method/function/trait/impl generic declarations.

Trait encoding computes `generic_names` but does not use them when serializing associated-type bounds/defaults, associated-const types, or supertrait bounds, although decoding now validates all of those fields with that context. A trait with generic `true` and an ambiguous field such as associated-const type `Option<true>` therefore encodes JSON that the decoder rejects. These fields need symmetric generic-aware encode validation.

The keyword normalizer preserves `where` only when its next token is an identifier. Valid nested clauses can instead begin with a lifetime or qualified type, such as `fn f<'a>() where 'a: 'static {}` or `where <T as Trait>::Assoc: Copy`. If the alias also declares a raw generic named `where`, the normalizer rewrites both the generic reference and this syntax token to `r#where`; normalized parsing fails, while fallback parsing fails on the unescaped generic reference. Valid aliases are therefore rejected at the conversion boundary.

Boolean-named generics behind `*mut` are incorrectly classified as ambiguous. For example, `Box<*mut true>` with a declared raw generic named `true` is unambiguously a type, but the scanner recognizes `*const` and not `*mut`, so conversion rejects a valid alias before normalization.

Non-alias `TypeEntry` generic declarations are serialized without encode-side validation. A struct or enum containing a malformed generic bound such as `T U` therefore encodes successfully, but decoding the resulting document rejects that same bound. Validate entry-level generics before converting methods, kind, and predicates to preserve codec symmetry.

`validate_generic_params_for_encode` validates bounds but never rejects duplicate names or method generics that shadow outer generics. Trait, function, impl, and method declarations can consequently encode duplicate/shadowing parameters that `method_generics_from_dtos_with_outer_generics` rejects when decoding the generated document.

Decode constructs generic parameters with `ParamName::new` and checks bounds and duplicates, but it does not apply the generic-name validation now enforced during encode. Because `ParamName` accepts `_`, a struct, trait, function, impl, or method with a generic named `_` can decode successfully, while encoding the resulting document rejects it. This also admits an illegal Rust declaration at the input boundary; apply the same `is_valid_generic_param_name` check to all decoded generic declarations.

The keyword normalizer still rewrites valid syntax when a raw generic has the same spelling. For example, `type Alias<r#async> = (r#async, [u8; { async unsafe fn f() {} 0 }]);` is valid, but the nested `async` is rewritten because only `async fn`, `async move`, and blocks are recognized. Stable `move` closures and `pub` nested items are likewise always rewritten by the default branch. The normalized parse then fails, and fallback parsing cannot parse the unescaped generic reference, so valid aliases are rejected.

This production-only module is now 701 lines, exceeding the repository's hard 700-line production-module limit. Split the encode validation/conversion helpers into a sibling module to restore the architecture constraint.

The keyword normalizer preserves only a subset of valid `async`/`const` syntax. For example, with a normalized raw generic named `async`, the valid alias target `(async, [u8; { async extern "C" fn f() {} 0 }])` rewrites the nested item keyword to `r#async`; `async ||` closures and `const extern` functions fail similarly. The normalized parse then fails, while the fallback cannot parse the unescaped generic occurrence, so extended-crate encoding rejects valid source-derived aliases. Preserve the complete function-qualifier and async-closure contexts before restoring keyword generics.

`should_restore` still rewrites several stable Rust syntax occurrences as generic identifiers. For example, a valid source alias with generic `r#unsafe` and target `(r#unsafe, [u8; { unsafe trait Marker {} 0 }])` is normalized into a target containing `r#unsafe trait`, so both parse attempts fail. The same problem remains for `static mut` and `pub union`; postfix `.await` is silently changed to `.r#await`, altering the encoded array-length expression. This causes valid rustdoc-normalized aliases to be rejected or structurally corrupted. Recognize these stable syntax contexts before restoring raw generic spelling.

The generic-keyword restorer still misclassifies raw-pointer `mut` as a generic reference. For a valid alias such as `type Alias<r#mut> = (r#mut, *mut u8);`, rustdoc's normalized target `(mut, *mut u8)` is rewritten to `(r#mut, *r#mut u8)` because `binding_modifier_syntax` does not recognize a preceding `*`. The rewritten parse fails, and the original normalized spelling cannot serve as fallback because its first `mut` is not a valid type, so the infrastructure adapter rejects a valid catalogue entry. Preserve `mut` after `*` and add an end-to-end regression test.

Keyword restoration still misclassifies several stable Rust syntax positions as generic references. For example, with a declared generic named `as`, the valid Edition-2024 alias `type A<r#as> = (r#as, [u8; { fn f() { let _ = 0usize as *const u8; } 0 }]);` reaches the codec without `r#`; the cast operator is rewritten to `r#as`, so the normalized parse fails, while fallback parsing fails on the outer bare generic. The current match arms similarly reject valid aliases containing `for &pattern`, `use ::path`, `unsafe static`, or `async move {}` alongside the corresponding keyword-named generic. Make syntax-position recognition complete for these stable forms and add end-to-end cases.

Inside brace groups, several branches unconditionally preserve keywords as syntax, even when they occur in raw-identifier positions. A valid alias such as `type A<r#if> = (r#if, [u8; { fn f<r#if>() {} 0 }]);` is normalized to use bare `if`; the inner generic declaration is left unchanged because `in_const_group` is true, making the normalized parse fail, and fallback also fails on the outer bare `if`. The same problem affects `let`, `match`, `while`, `loop`, `else`, `return`, `break`, `continue`, and `in`. Disambiguate their actual token position within brace groups instead of treating every occurrence as control-flow syntax.

Keyword normalization misclassifies a valid `for` loop whose irrefutable pattern is a bracket group. For example, with generic parameter `r#for`, a target containing `for [x] in [[1]]` rewrites the loop keyword to `r#for`; the normalized parse then fails, while fallback parsing fails on the other rustdoc-normalized generic references, rejecting a valid catalogue type.

`inside_angle_group` treats every unmatched `<` token as a generic delimiter, including comparison operators. In a valid const expression such as `1 < if !false { 2 } else { 3 }`, the `if` is consequently treated as a generic identifier and rewritten to `r#if`. When the target also contains a normalized keyword generic, both the normalized and fallback parses fail, rejecting valid input.

The `use` branch preserves any `use` followed by `:` inside a const group, so a rustdoc-normalized raw generic projection such as `r#use::Assoc` remains the invalid spelling `use::Assoc`. A valid target containing a nested `fn f<r#use: Tr>(_: r#use::Assoc)` therefore fails normalized parsing, and fallback parsing also fails on other normalized `use` generic references.

The const-block keyword guard loses the surrounding type context when recursion enters a nested group. For example, the valid alias target `(if, [u8; { type X<if> = (if,); 0 }])` with generic `if` restores the declaration's `<if>` but leaves the nested tuple's `if` as a keyword, so both the normalized parse and original fallback fail. Valid aliases containing nested type items are therefore rejected.

Named bare-function arguments bypass `normalized_ident_name`. For `type A<r#if> = fn(r#if: r#if) -> r#if`, normalization makes syn retain the name as `r#if`, and this code emits that spelling even though rustdoc/catalogue identifiers use `if`, causing structural-equality mismatches.

Boolean ambiguity validation disables all type-position recognition inside const groups, including unambiguous nested generic declarations. The valid target `(true, C<{ type X<true> = (true,); 0 }>)` with generic `true` is rejected at `<true>` before normalization, so valid raw-identifier aliases cannot be encoded.

The syntax-keyword lookahead recognizes only a subset of valid Rust expression starts. For example, with a generic named `match`, the valid target `(match, C<{ match 0 { _ => 0 } }>)` rewrites the inner `match` to `r#match` because a literal is not accepted here. The normalized parse then fails, while the original fallback cannot parse the outer normalized generic reference, so the valid alias is rejected.

Boolean ambiguity validation treats every parenthesized group encountered at positive angle depth as a type-tuple context, even when it is inside an explicit const block. Thus `(true, C<{ (true) }>)` with generic `true` passes validation and the normalizer rewrites the boolean literal to `r#true`; the adapter emits a const path with `is_literal=false` instead of the source boolean literal, causing incorrect structural comparison rather than failing closed.

The nested generic-declaration detector omits `union`. A valid alias containing `union X<r#true> { value: ManuallyDrop<r#true> }` inside an anonymous const is normalized to `union X<true> ...`, but `<true>` is classified as an ambiguous const argument and rejected before raw-identifier restoration. Include union declarations in this declaration-position check.
